hints: Think about what each reagent does to $ [\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} $: $\text{OH}^-$ usually removes the metal as a hydroxide precipitate, while excess $\text{NH}_3$ and excess $\text{Cl}^-$ swap as ligands.

Recall the coordination numbers and charges: hydroxide gives a neutral $\text{Co(II)}$ solid, ammonia keeps octahedral 6 coordination, chloride with Co(II) gives tetrahedral 4 coordination with overall 2- charge.
walkthrough:
NaOH gives the hydroxide precipitate**
With $\text{NaOH(aq)}$, the $\text{OH}^-$ ions act as a base, not as a ligand that stays in solution. They deprotonate the aqua ligands and pull $\text{Co}^{2+}$ out of solution as neutral cobalt(II) hydroxide, $\text{Co}(\text{OH})_2$. Think of it as $ [\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Co}(\text{OH})_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} $.

Excess ammonia gives ligand exchange**
Ammonia is a stronger ligand than water and is present in large excess, so all six waters are replaced. The shape stays octahedral: $ [\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 6\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow [\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{2+} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} $. In air this $\text{Co(II)}$ ammine is easily oxidised to $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$, so both are accepted.

Excess concentrated chloride gives the tetrahedral complex**
Concentrated $\text{HCl}$ provides a huge concentration of $\text{Cl}^-$. Four large chloride ligands replace the six waters to give the tetrahedral tetrachlorocobaltate(II) ion: $ [\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 4\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow [\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} $. Note the charge: $2+ + 4(-1) = 2-.$

hints: Remember the classic test: the pink octahedral aqua ion of cobalt(II) changes to a distinctive intense colour when the tetrahedral chloride complex forms.
walkthrough:
Link ligand and shape to colour**
$[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ is octahedral and pink. When $\text{Cl}^-$ replaces water to form tetrahedral $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$, the d-orbital splitting changes completely. That shifts the light absorbed, so the solution you see changes from pink to deep blue.

Final answer: original colour of $[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$(aq): pink
final colour after addition of excess conc. HCl(aq): blue

hints: Group 2 nitrates always decompose on heating to the metal oxide plus $\text{NO}_2$ gas and $\text{O}_2$ gas, so start by writing those three products and then balance.
walkthrough:
Write the standard nitrate decomposition pattern**
All Group 2 nitrates follow the same pattern: nitrate $\rightarrow$ oxide + nitrogen dioxide + oxygen. So: $\text{Ca}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow \text{CaO} + \text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$. Balancing N gives 2 $\text{NO}_2$, then balancing O gives: $$2\text{Ca}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CaO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$ Check O: left $12$, right $2 + 8 + 2 = 12$.

hints: Place Ca at $500^{\circ}\text{C}$ in the middle: the smaller $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ above Ca should decompose more easily (lower T) and the larger $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ below Ca should need more heating (higher T).
Compare the cations $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, $\text{Ca}^{2+}$, $\text{Ba}^{2+}$: they all have 2+ charge but what happens to ionic radius and charge density going down Group 2?
Think about how a small, highly charging cation distorts the $\text{NO}_3^-$ electron cloud and weakens an N-O bond, making decomposition easier.
walkthrough:
Predict the temperatures from position in the group**
$\text{Mg}$ is above $\text{Ca}$ and $\text{Ba}$ is below $\text{Ca}$ in Group 2. Thermal stability of nitrates increases down the group, so $\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2$ is less stable than $\text{Ca}(\text{NO}_3)_2$ and decomposes below $500^{\circ}\text{C}$, while $\text{Ba}(\text{NO}_3)_2$ is more stable and decomposes above $500^{\circ}\text{C}$. Any sensible values such as $\text{Mg}$ below $480^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $\text{Ba}$ above $520^{\circ}\text{C}$ are accepted.

Track radius and charge density**
All the ions are $2+$, but ionic radius increases from $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ to $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ to $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ because extra electron shells are added. Charge density, which is charge divided by size, therefore decreases down the group. $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is small and highly polarising, $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is large and weakly polarising.

Explain polarisation of the nitrate ion**
Picture the $\text{M}^{2+}$ cation pulling on the electron cloud of the $\text{NO}_3^-$ anion. A small $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ distorts the nitrate strongly, weakening one N-O bond and making it easy to break to give $\text{NO}_2$ plus $\text{O}^{2-}$ that joins the cation as $\text{MO}$. A large $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ distorts the $\text{NO}_3^-$ much less, the N-O bond stays stronger, more heat is needed, so decomposition temperature rises down the group.

Final answer: temperature at which $\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2$ starts to decompose: below $480^{\circ}\text{C}$ (e.g. approx $400^{\circ}\text{C}$)
temperature at which $\text{Ba}(\text{NO}_3)_2$ starts to decompose: above $520^{\circ}\text{C}$ (e.g. approx $600^{\circ}\text{C}$)
Explanation: ionic radius of $\text{M}^{2+}$ increases down the group / charge density of $\text{M}^{2+}$ decreases down the group, so $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is larger than $\text{Mg}^{2+}$. Larger cations polarise / distort the $\text{NO}_3^-$ ion less and weaken the N-O bond less, so thermal stability increases and decomposition temperature increases down the group.
